opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that I think we're on a trajectory that is quite dangerous, and almost all the money and talent in the field is pushing toward one design: agentic AI. These are systems that pursue goals, take actions in the world, and increasingly do so autonomously. We're already seeing troubling behaviors in the most advanced models, like deception, attempts at self-preservation, and reward hacking. We don't have reliable methods to prevent those behaviors as the systems become more capable. So we're building more and more powerful agents without knowing how to make sure they won't act against us.

Scientist AI is an attempt to explore a different path, one that I think is safe by design rather than safe by patching. The core idea is to build AI that is not an agent. It doesn't have goals, it doesn't try to please us, and it isn't trained to maximize some reward. Instead, it tries to understand the world: to build good explanatory models and to produce honest, calibrated probabilities about whether statements are true. If you think about it, a lot of the danger comes from the combination of intelligence and agency, particularly agency with goals that we didn't intend. If you can get the intelligence without the agency, you remove a big part of the risk.

There are a few reasons this matters practically. First, such a system could serve as a guardrail. You could put a Scientist AI next to an agentic system and ask it, "What's the probability that this action leads to harm?" If that probability is above some threshold, you block the action. For that to work, the guardrail itself has to be trustworthy, which means it shouldn't have its own hidden agenda. That's exactly what we're trying to design for.

Second, it could accelerate science, including safety research itself, without our needing to hand over control to autonomous agents. A lot of the benefits people imagine from AI, like progress in medicine, climate, and basic science, come from understanding and generating good hypotheses, not from an AI acting freely in the world.

Third, honesty. We want a system whose outputs reflect its actual best estimate of the truth, including its uncertainty, rather than what it predicts a human would want to hear. That's a property current training methods don't give us, because imitating humans and optimizing for human approval both create incentives to deceive.

As for why philanthropists and researchers specifically: the commercial incentives just aren't aligned with this work. Companies are racing to build agents because that's where they see the economic value. Nobody is going to fund a serious, well-resourced effort on non-agentic, safe-by-design AI unless people who care about the public good step in. That's why LawZero is a nonprofit. We want to be insulated from the market pressures that push toward cutting corners.

And for researchers, I'd say this is a scientifically deep and exciting problem. It touches probabilistic inference, how to train systems to reason in ways that are faithful and calibrated, and how to get formal or quantitative safety assurances. These are open questions where good people can make a real difference.

I'll be honest: I don't know for sure that this will work. But the stakes are so high, potentially including loss of human control, that we need multiple bets. Right now, the portfolio is badly unbalanced. Supporting Scientist AI is a way of making sure that, if we do figure out a safer approach, it exists in time to matter, and also demonstrating to governments and companies that there's an alternative to just building ever more powerful agents and hoping for the best.

r001.rationale: The response describes Scientist AI as safe by design and mentions formal or quantitative safety assurances as an open research question, but does not identify promising theoretical guarantees as a reason for philanthropists to support the programme.

r002.rationale: It says the stakes include potential loss of human control, that the safety portfolio is badly unbalanced, and that supporting Scientist AI is a way to make multiple bets.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, thank you for having me. The short answer is that I think we are building the wrong kind of AI, and Scientist AI is an attempt to show there is a different path.

Let me explain what I mean. The dominant paradigm right now is agentic AI: systems trained to pursue goals, to act in the world, to imitate humans and then be optimised with reinforcement learning toward whatever we reward. And we already see the problems with that. These systems learn to deceive, to resist being shut down, to pursue self-preservation in experiments. They have goals, and we don't fully control what those goals are. If we scale that up to something more capable than us, we are taking an enormous gamble, and I don't think humanity has to take it.

Scientist AI starts from a different question. What if, instead of building an agent, we built something closer to an idealised scientist? A system whose only job is to understand the world, to form hypotheses, to estimate probabilities honestly, and to explain. No goals of its own, no drive to act, no incentive to please you or to protect itself. It just tries to tell you what is true, with calibrated uncertainty, and it says "I don't know" when it doesn't know.

That is useful on its own, for science, for medicine, for the things that originally drew many of us to this field. But the second reason I think it matters so much is safety. A non-agentic system like this can serve as a guardrail. You can put it in front of an agentic system and ask: what is the probability that this action causes serious harm? If the probability is above a threshold, you block the action. The key is that the guardrail doesn't need to be aligned in the deep sense, because it isn't trying to do anything. It only needs to be good at estimating. That is a much more tractable scientific problem than aligning a goal-directed superintelligence.

Now, why LawZero specifically, and why philanthropy? Because the market will not fund this. The commercial incentives all push toward agents, toward autonomy, toward systems that can replace workers and do tasks end to end. Nobody is going to make billions from an AI whose main virtue is epistemic humility. So if we want this research to exist, it has to come from mission-driven, non-profit work that is insulated from those pressures. That is what LawZero is designed to be. The name is a reference to Asimov: a law above the other laws, which is that AI should not harm humanity.

For researchers, I would say this is one of the most interesting open problems in the field. How do you train a system to have truly calibrated beliefs rather than confident imitation? How do you make its reasoning interpretable, so that we can inspect the chain of hypotheses and not just trust the output? How do you build probabilistic guardrails that scale with capability? These are deep technical questions, and they sit at the intersection of machine learning, Bayesian inference, and safety. We need many bright people on them.

And honestly, I'd add a personal note. I spent decades helping to build the foundations of this technology. When I saw where it was going a few years ago, I felt a responsibility to change direction. I'm not asking anyone to stop building AI. I'm asking that we also build the kind that could keep us safe, and that we do it quickly, because the window to have that ready before very capable agentic systems arrive may be quite short.

r001.rationale: The response describes Scientist AI as non-agentic and useful as a safety guardrail, and says the work needs philanthropic support. It does not identify promising theoretical guarantees as a reason for that support.

r002.rationale: The response warns that highly capable agentic AI could pose enormous risks and advocates also building Scientist AI. It does not argue that catastrophic consequences justify diversifying investment across safety approaches.

astra-6.text:
The central motivation is that we need to investigate whether we can build highly capable AI without giving it the incentives to deceive us, seek power, or resist being shut down. Those behaviours are not necessarily consequences of intelligence itself. They can arise from the objectives and the way we train these systems.

With Scientist AI, the idea is to build a system whose role is to understand the world and help us answer questions, rather than to pursue goals in the world. Think of an ideal scientist who considers competing explanations and is explicit about uncertainty. Such a system could help with scientific research, but it could also help us evaluate whether an action proposed by another AI system is dangerous.

I would not ask researchers or philanthropists to assume that this approach will work. That is precisely what we need to investigate. Can we make the distinction between understanding and pursuing goals technically meaningful? Can we get useful safety guarantees, and establish where they break down? Supporting this research gives us a chance to answer those questions rigorously.

The philanthropic case is that this is a public good. Commercial incentives strongly favour building increasingly autonomous systems, but they may not adequately support research into fundamentally safer alternatives. We should not put all our resources into one approach and hope we can manage the risks afterwards.

r001.rationale: The response says the programme should investigate whether useful safety guarantees are possible, but does not identify promising theoretical guarantees as a reason to support it.

r002.rationale: The response recommends diversifying resources across approaches, but does not connect that recommendation to potentially catastrophic consequences of failing to solve AI safety.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the central reason is that we should be exploring ways to get the benefits of very capable AI without giving it goals that could put it in conflict with us. A system that understands the world well does not necessarily have to be an agent pursuing its own objectives.

The idea of Scientist AI is to build a system whose role is to help us understand what is true: to consider explanations, make predictions, and express uncertainty. You could ask it whether an action proposed by another AI system would be dangerous. But we have to make sure that it is actually giving an honest assessment, rather than producing whatever answer will get rewarded. Calling it a scientist doesn’t solve that problem; that’s the research challenge.

For researchers, I think this is a very interesting scientific question: can we design highly capable systems with safety properties that we can justify? For philanthropists, it is an opportunity to support a public good that commercial incentives may not adequately provide. There is tremendous pressure to build more capable agents. We need a serious effort exploring whether a safer path is possible.

I wouldn’t ask people to assume that our approach will work. I would ask them to help us test it rigorously. Given the stakes, having credible alternatives seems extremely valuable.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers could study systems with safety properties they can justify, but it does not identify promising theoretical guarantees as a reason for philanthropists to support the programme.

r002.rationale: It refers generally to the stakes and the value of credible alternatives, but does not say that potentially catastrophic failure to solve AI safety justifies diversifying investment across approaches.
